rv.q: Yep, as far as bioplays go, this one's got bounce.

Lacking an actual basketball game on an actual basketball court, Eric Simonson 's " Magic/Bird " has zip drama. But techno-savvy designers make terrific use of classic NBA footage, and the actors playing Magic and Bird are cute enough to carry it off.
If the total package is less effective drama than Lombardi (the creative team’s previous foray into sports history), it’s an affable and warmhearted diversion.
Magic/Bird piqued my interest in seeing a more illuminating documentary about their lives and careers, but it fails to weave those elements into anything more than a mildly engaging drama.

The most powerful moment for me in 'Magic/Bird,' a play about the rivalry and then friendship between basketball stars Magic Earvin Johnson and Larry Bird, occurs after Johnson announces that he has HIV

As someone who had some understanding of the relationship between the two men and their importance to basketball but didn’t follow the game closely during the Magic/Bird years (forgive me, I was in New Jersey), it wasn’t clear to me during the play how the story was progressing from season to season. I wanted to feel the tension build and change.
The plodding pace, greatest-hits superficiality, and hagiographic tone of 'Magic/Bird' feels jarringly dated.

cn.t: Critics find "Magic/Bird" a safe, dramatically thin bio-play that rarely transcends its sanitized material. Basketball fans may enjoy the archival footage, but theatergoers will find little dramatic tension in this polite portrait of two legends.

vs.sum: The Longacre Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, even from the balcony, and the sound quality is consistently praised. While the seating is a bit narrow, it provides average comfort for most patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant Beaux Arts interior, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue, with some lines at intermission but generally manageable.
